test_text.title: What's the purpose of gaining knowledge?

article.title: What's the purpose of gaining knowledge?

items.sentence_raw: "I would found an institution where any person can find instruction in any subject."
That was the founder's motto for Cornell University, and it seems an apt characterization of the different university, also in the USA, where I currently teach philosophy.
A student can prepare for a career in resort management, engineering, interior design, accounting, music, law enforcement, you name it.
But what would the founders of these two institutions have thought of a course called "Arson for Profit"?
items.explain: Q27: The passage asks what the founders would think of a course called *'Arson for Profit'* — this is a **surprising course title**. So the heading is **vi**.

items.sentence_raw: I kid you not: we have it on the books.
Any undergraduates who have met the academic requirements can sign up for the course in our program in "fire science".
items.explain: Q33: The passage says undergraduates can sign up for the course in the program in *'fire science'* — so they are studying **fire science**.

items.sentence_raw: Naturally, the course is intended for prospective arson investigators, who can learn all the tricks of the trade for detecting whether a fire was deliberately set, discovering who did it, and establishing a chain of evidence for effective prosecution in a court of law.
items.explain:
Q34: The passage says the course is for *'prospective arson investigators'* — so they will become **investigators** or **arson investigators**.

Q35: The passage says the course teaches how to establish a *'chain of evidence'* — so they find **evidence** of criminal intent.

Q36: The passage says the evidence is for effective *'prosecution'* in court — so it leads to successful **prosecution**.

items.sentence_raw: But wouldn't this also be the perfect course for prospective arsonists to sign up for?
items.explain:
Q28: The passage asks if this course would also be perfect for *'prospective arsonists'* — this means it might attract the **wrong kind of student**. So the heading is **viii**.

Q38: The passage asks if this course would be perfect for *'prospective arsonists'* — people who set fires. This directly confirms the statement, so the answer is **YES**.

items.sentence_raw: My point is not to criticize academic programs in fire science: they are highly welcome as part of the increasing professionalization of this and many other occupations.
items.explain: Q39: The passage says fire science courses are *'highly welcome'* for professionalization — this means they are **not too academic** and do help people be good at the job. The statement says the opposite, so the answer is **NO**.

items.sentence_raw: However, it's not unknown for a firefighter to torch a building.
This example suggests how dishonest and illegal behavior, with the help of higher education, can creep into every aspect of public and business life.
I realized this anew when I was invited to speak before a class in marketing, which is another of our degree programs.
The regular instructor is a colleague who appreciates the kind of ethical perspective I can bring as a philosopher.
There are endless ways I could have approached this assignment, but I took my cue from the title of the course: "Principles of Marketing".
items.explain: Q29: The writer says he took his cue from the course title *'Principles of Marketing'* — **'principles'** can mean rules or ethics, so the title has **two meanings**. So the heading is **ii**.

items.sentence_raw: It made me think to ask the students, "Is marketing principled?"
After all, a subject matter can have principles in the sense of being codified, having rules, as with football or chess, without being principled in the sense of being ethical.
Many of the students immediately assumed that the answer to my question about marketing principles was obvious: "no".
Just look at the ways in which everything under the sun has been marketed; obviously it need not be done in a "principled" (=ethical) fashion.
Is that obvious?
I made the suggestion, which may sound downright crazy in light of the evidence, that perhaps marketing is "by definition" principled.
My inspiration for this judgement is the philosopher Immanuel Kant, who argued that any body of knowledge consists of an end (or purpose) and a means.
items.explain: Q30: The writer uses Kant's idea that knowledge has an **end** and a **means** — he applies this theory to marketing, which is an **unexpected context**. So the heading is **iv**.

items.sentence_raw: Let us apply both the terms "means" and "end" to marketing.
The students have signed up for a course in order to learn how to market effectively.
But to what "end"?
There seem to be two main attitudes toward that question.
One is that the answer is obvious: the purpose of marketing is to sell things and to make money.

The other attitude is that the "purpose" of marketing is irrelevant: Each person comes to the program and course with his or her own plans, and these need not even concern the acquisition of marketing expertise as such.
My proposal, which I believe would also be Kant's, is that "neither" of these attitudes captures the significance of the end to the means for marketing.
A field of knowledge or a professional endeavor is defined by both the means "and" the end; hence "both" deserve scrutiny.
items.explain: Q31: The passage says a field is defined by both the **means** *'and'* the **end**, and *'both'* deserve scrutiny — this shows the **equal importance of two key issues**. So the heading is **iii**.

items.sentence_raw: Students need to study both how to achieve X, and also what X is.
It is at this point that "Arson for Profit" becomes supremely relevant.
That course is presumably all about "means": how to detect and prosecute criminal activity.
It is therefore assumed that the "end" is good in an ethical sense.
When I ask fire science students to articulate the end, or purpose, of their field, they eventually generalize to something like, "The safety and welfare of society," which seems right.
items.explain: Q40: The passage says students *'eventually generalize'* to a purpose like *'The safety and welfare of society'* — this is a general idea, not a **detailed definition**. So the answer is **NO**.

items.sentence_raw: As we have seen, someone could use the very same knowledge of "means" to achieve a much less noble end, such as personal profit via destructive, dangerous, reckless activity.
But "we would not call that firefighting".
items.explain: Q32: The passage says using fire knowledge for bad ends is called *'arson'*, not firefighting, and bad marketing is called *'fraud'* — these are **different names for different outcomes**. So the heading is **vii**.

items.sentence_raw: We have a separate word for it: "arson".
items.explain: Q32: The passage says using fire knowledge for bad ends is called *'arson'*, not firefighting, and bad marketing is called *'fraud'* — these are **different names for different outcomes**. So the heading is **vii**.

items.sentence_raw: Similarly, if you employed the "principles of marketing" in an unprincipled way, "you would not be doing marketing".
items.explain: Q32: The passage says using fire knowledge for bad ends is called *'arson'*, not firefighting, and bad marketing is called *'fraud'* — these are **different names for different outcomes**. So the heading is **vii**.

items.sentence_raw: We have another term for it: "fraud".

items.sentence_raw: Kant gives the example of a doctor and a poisoner, who use the identical knowledge to achieve their divergent ends.
We would say that one is practicing medicine, the other, murder.

orphan_explain_map.37: Q37: The passage talks about many career-focused courses, but it never says it is **difficult** to attract students to non-career courses. This information is missing, so the answer is **NOT GIVEN**.
